coordinateNote: Map markers identify approximate building centres or entrance areas unless noted. Use the verified address and official visitor information to plan access.

locations.name: Cathédrale Notre-Dame de Paris
locations.address: 6 Parvis Notre-Dame – Place Jean-Paul II, 75004 Paris
locations.history: Notre-Dame's Gothic architecture creates space for monumental stained glass. Its three rose windows combine geometric construction with Christian imagery.
locations.symbols: Christian iconography and circular geometric construction are documented features of the windows.
locations.interpretation: CAISIK reading: many perspectives can belong to one structure. This contemporary analogy does not establish an alchemical construction programme.
locations.observe: Compare the rose window's circle with the façade's vertical divisions. Find repetition, symmetry and departures from symmetry.
locations.reflection: Which frame changes what you notice?
locations.challenge: Write four bars using stone, light, circle and memory without saying cathedral.
locations.access: Cathedral admission is free with or without a reservation. Use the official reservation system and respect worship and current entry instructions.
locations.accessibility: The central portal is wheelchair accessible. The official accessibility page describes internal arrangements; this does not apply to the towers.

locations.name: Sainte-Chapelle
locations.history: Commissioned by Louis IX within the Palais de la Cité, Sainte-Chapelle uses stained-glass narratives and royal imagery to express religious and political authority.
locations.symbols: Fleurs-de-lis, Castilian castles, coronation scenes and biblical narratives are documented by the monument operator.
locations.interpretation: CAISIK reading: daylight changes the architecture you perceive. This is a reflection on perception, not an undocumented occult alignment.
locations.observe: Find a repeated royal emblem in a window border and compare its scale with the narrative scenes.
locations.reflection: Who controls the story when images surround you?
locations.challenge: Sketch a four-panel transformation story with one recurring symbol.
locations.access: Ticket and timed reservation required. Security rules apply inside the Palais de Justice perimeter; aerosols, sharp objects and bulky luggage are prohibited.
locations.accessibility: The operator states that the tour is accessible to visitors with reduced mobility. Consult its detailed arrangements before visiting.

locations.name: Maison de Nicolas Flamel
locations.history: The house dates to 1407. Nicolas Flamel was a Parisian writer and property owner. His reputation as a successful alchemist developed after his death.
locations.symbols: The façade and dated religious inscription are historical evidence; alchemical narratives belong to Flamel's later reception.
locations.interpretation: A real person becomes a cultural legend. This building is not a verified secret laboratory.
locations.observe: Separate what the dated inscription says from the stories attached to its patron.
locations.reflection: Which parts of an identity are evidence, and which are repeated stories?
locations.challenge: Write two couplets: first the documented person, then the myth.
locations.access: View the exterior from the public street. A restaurant occupies the building; there is no general permission to enter private rooms.
locations.accessibility: Interior accessibility has not been verified. Assess the exterior pavement on site.

locations.name: Saint-Sulpice — Gnomon
locations.history: Astronomers from the Observatoire de Paris installed the precision gnomon in agreement with the parish priest in 1743.
locations.symbols: The meridian line and obelisk are components of an astronomical instrument, not evidence of a secret society.
locations.interpretation: CAISIK reading: a line connects human measurement with a changing sky. The analogy is contemporary; the astronomical purpose is documented.
locations.observe: Follow the meridian line toward the obelisk. Consider how sunlight becomes a measurement.
locations.reflection: What gives your life rhythm: a clock or deliberate attention?
locations.challenge: Write four bars, each beginning at a different time of day.
locations.access: Active church. Confirm the parish's current gnomon-visit programme; group visits require prior agreement. Crypt and upper-area visits have separate conditions.
locations.accessibility: Step-free access has not been verified. Contact the parish for a visit-specific assessment.

locations.name: Cimetière du Père-Lachaise
locations.coordinateStatus: Approximate rue du Repos entrance area
locations.history: Père-Lachaise combines an active cemetery with a significant heritage of funerary architecture and sculpture. It remains a place of mourning.
locations.symbols: Study religious figures, portraits, inscriptions and allegories individually. Funerary motifs do not all have one universal meaning.
locations.interpretation: Memento mori is a reflective lens, not proof that every monument belongs to one hidden doctrine.
locations.observe: Describe one monument's material, posture and inscription before interpreting it.
locations.reflection: What would you want the city to remember about you?
locations.challenge: Write an eight-line remembrance poem quietly; record it elsewhere.
locations.access: Free cemetery with seasonal hours. Evacuation starts 15 minutes before closing. Respect graves and ceremonies. The Héloïse and Abélard monument is under restoration until August 2027 according to the city.
locations.accessibility: The city lists reduced-mobility access but warns of uneven, narrow paths and difficult areas. Amandiers and Réunion entrances have stairs; the full route is not assured accessible.

sources.title: City of Paris — access, hours and current works

locations.name: Monument à la République
locations.history: Installed in 1883, the monument places Marianne above allegories of Liberty, Equality and Fraternity. Twelve bronze reliefs depict episodes in French republican history.
locations.symbols: Marianne personifies the Republic. The three surrounding allegories represent the national motto.
locations.interpretation: CAISIK reading: compare enduring ideals in stone with the square's changing uses. Keep contemporary reflection separate from the documented programme.
locations.observe: Identify the three allegories and follow the historical reliefs around the pedestal.
locations.reflection: When does a public symbol become part of your own experience?
locations.challenge: Write a call-and-response between an ideal and street-level reality.
locations.access: Outdoor public square. Temporary events, policing or works can affect access.
locations.accessibility: No route-wide accessibility guarantee verified; assess the current outdoor conditions.

locations.name: Abbesses — Guimard Entrance
locations.history: Hector Guimard designed the covered Art Nouveau entrance. Originally at Hôtel-de-Ville, it moved to Abbesses in 1974; it was not the station's original Nord-Sud entrance.
locations.symbols: Organic ironwork and lettering are Art Nouveau design features. The station's underlying decoration belongs to the Nord-Sud system.
locations.interpretation: CAISIK reading: infrastructure can suggest a living organism through line and typography. This is an artistic analogy.
locations.observe: Trace the transition from supporting ironwork into ornament and lettering.
locations.reflection: How does an entrance change your expectations of what lies below?
locations.challenge: Sketch THRESHOLD as a handstyle using one organic curve.
locations.access: View the exterior from the square. Transport access requires the appropriate fare and current service availability.
locations.accessibility: Station lifts do not establish a step-free platform route. Verify transport accessibility separately with RATP.

locations.name: Le M.U.R. Oberkampf
locations.address: 107 rue Oberkampf, corner of rue Saint-Maur, 75011 Paris
locations.coordinateStatus: Approximate wall position corroborated by published coordinates
locations.history: Le M.U.R. is an association-led urban-art programme presenting successive temporary works on a large panel at the Oberkampf and Saint-Maur corner.
locations.symbols: Interpret each changing work through its named artist and documentation. No single motif permanently defines the wall.
locations.interpretation: CAISIK reading: a wall can preserve cultural memory while its surface keeps changing.
locations.observe: Record the artist, date and composition, then compare with a later visit.
locations.reflection: Does disappearance reduce an artwork's value or intensify the encounter?
locations.challenge: Respond on paper with one letter carrying an architectural and emotional meaning.
locations.access: Outdoor viewing. This is a curated, authorized exhibition wall, not a free-paint wall. Painting requires explicit organizer permission.
locations.accessibility: Street-level viewing; pavement and crowd conditions vary. Formal accessibility has not been verified.

locations.name: La Place — Centre culturel hip-hop
locations.coordinateStatus: Verified destination coordinates in official La Place site Google Maps link
locations.history: La Place supports hip-hop expression, transmission and artistic creation through concerts, exhibitions, workshops and dedicated creation spaces.
locations.symbols: Music, dance, graffiti, image and audiovisual practice are explicit parts of the centre's mission.
locations.interpretation: Inner alchemy is CAISIK's metaphor for expression and practice, not a doctrine attributed to the centre.
locations.observe: Consider the rehearsal, recording and exchange that make a performance possible.
locations.reflection: What changes when private practice becomes shared culture?
locations.challenge: Write sixteen bars about your city route, then review one breath and one flow choice.
locations.access: Check the official agenda for event tickets and entry. Studios need a separate booking; unrestricted drop-in studio access is not implied.
locations.accessibility: Confirm room- and event-specific requirements directly with the venue.

locations.name: CENTQUATRE-PARIS
locations.coordinateStatus: Approximate venue centre; official site links OpenStreetMap way 278632326
locations.history: Built in 1874 for Paris funeral services, the complex later passed through a period of urbex and street art before reopening as an arts institution in 2008.
locations.symbols: Industrial halls and former funerary functions are documented history. Artistic reuse changes the material purpose of the site.
locations.interpretation: CAISIK reading: transformation need not erase a place's former life.
locations.observe: Compare the repetition of the halls with the individual movements of people practising inside.
locations.reflection: What from your past could support new work?
locations.challenge: Repeat one industrial rhythm in three movement or drawing variations.
locations.access: Public halls follow published opening hours; events and exhibitions may need tickets. Follow house rules and obtain agreement before recording practitioners.
locations.accessibility: The venue confirms accessible ground-floor crossing and performance rooms. Some other spaces require staff assistance.

locations.name: Philharmonie de Paris
locations.history: Jean Nouvel's Philharmonie opened in 2015 within the La Villette cultural landscape. Its exterior combines mineral forms with a repeated bird pavement.
locations.symbols: The bird forms and dialogue with the park are described by the operator. They are not evidence of undocumented sacred geometry.
locations.interpretation: CAISIK reading: repeated individual units can suggest collective movement, like voices inside a music scene.
locations.observe: Follow one bird shape into its neighbours, then compare that repetition with the building's larger contours.
locations.challenge: Turn a pattern into four beats, then vary the final beat.
locations.access: Architectural viewing, concerts, exhibitions and the belvedere have different access conditions and schedules. Verify the intended visit with the operator.
locations.accessibility: Consult official visitor information for room-specific arrangements. No always-open rooftop route is implied.

locations.name: Shakespeare and Company
locations.history: George Whitman founded the present English-language bookshop here in 1951. It is distinct from Sylvia Beach's earlier shop at another address.
locations.symbols: Books, reading spaces and a continuing literary programme provide the cultural context. No occult connection is claimed.
locations.interpretation: CAISIK reading: an independent bookshop is an archive kept alive by reading, writing and gathering.
locations.observe: Notice how shelves, signs and room proportions guide attention. Observe without photographing inside.
locations.reflection: Which sentence could become a doorway?
locations.challenge: Outside, write a four-line scene using a new word and a street detail.
locations.access: Check hours and event closures. Large groups and large bags are restricted. Photography and filming inside are prohibited.
locations.accessibility: Most of the ground floor, the Antiquarian bookshop and café are wheelchair accessible according to the operator. This is not an all-floors guarantee; ask staff for assistance.
